citation.title: The Frankfort-mandibular incisor angle (FMIA) in orthodontic diagnosis, treatment planning and prognosis

curation.notes: Compared 2026-10-08 (norms:compare a vs b exit 1). Means agree in both (24.57, 86.93, 68.2, n 95). Differences settled from the page images (scan, no text layer): (1) range only in b (FMA 15-36, IMPA 76-99, FMIA 56-80) -> kept: Chart I, p. 138 (PDF page 18) prints these as its column headings '(15° to 36°)', '(76° to 99°)', '(56° to 80°)', and the lowest/highest rows with a non-zero count match (FMA 15 n 5 / 36 n 1; IMPA 76 n 1 / 99 n 2; FMIA 56 n 1 / 80 n 2); each count column sums to the printed TOTAL 95. (2) source wording -> one wording naming Chart I (AVERAGE row and Range heading, p. 138) and text p. 125. The averages read on the page image of p. 138 (AVERAGE row 24.57°, 86.93°, 68.20°) and of p. 125 ('FMA 24.57, IMPA 86.93 and FMIA 68.2'). (3) definitionMatch FMA and FMIA a=same b=close -> close (merge-notes ruling): p. 124 draws the Frankfort plane from a point 4½ mm above the geometric centre of the ear rod to the lower border of the orbit, also p. 138; IMPA same (axis through apex and incisal edge to the lower-border mandibular plane, p. 124). Prose: headPosition a=FH b=unknown -> unknown (the paper describes ear rods, never a head orientation); population reduced to the analysis-own defaults (Tucson moved into a caveat). Rulings applied: N1/P6 means = Tweed's printed 95-case averages, his rounded norms 24/87/69 (p. 138) in note, his targets in clinicalTarget; no SD (none printed; none invented); sample means, so no centre; scale not-stated (angles only; magnification-research.md).

caveats: Sample: 95 people chosen by Tweed in Tucson, Arizona, for pleasing balance of facial outline (p. 124: any malocclusion was not examined): club acquaintances, friends, parents of patients and a few of his older treated cases. Sex, age and ethnicity are not given; the illustrated samples include children and adults.
No SD is printed. Chart I (p. 138) gives the whole-degree frequency of each angle; the ranges entered are its column headings.

Tweed's Frankfort plane runs from a point 4.5 mm above the geometric centre of the ear rod to the lower border of the orbit (pp. 124, 138), not from anatomical porion; he says this tends to make the FMA smaller. FMA and FMIA are therefore 'close', not 'same'.
First 45 samples (p. 124): FMA 24.9°, IMPA 86.6°, FMIA 68.6° — superseded by the 95-sample averages, not entered.

Tweed's own recommendation from this sample (p. 138): adopt 24° for FMA, 87° for IMPA and 69° for FMIA as norms; given in each entry's note. His earlier norms (p. 124): FMA 25° (normal variation 20° to 30°), IMPA 90° (85° to 95°), FMIA 65°.

Not Tweed's sample, not entered: Downs's FMA 21.9° and IMPA 91.4° (p. 124); Brodie 1940's 11 cases, IMPA average 88.3° and Broadbent's Bolton composites 88.5° (3½ y), 83° (7 y), 89.5° (14 y), 92.5° (adults), average 88.4° (p. 125); the 37 illustrated samples IMPA 86.55° and FMA 24.913° (pp. 125, 138); IMPA 87.88° pooling Brodie, Broadbent and Tweed (p. 138).
Treatment results, not norms, not entered: averages after treatment of 37 consecutive cases FMA 27.54°, IMPA 86.5°, FMIA 67.01° (p. 139, Chart 2).
